title: The Last Lighthouse Keeper on the Coast
author: Ines Carvalho
date: 2026-08-09
extractor: trafilatura
---
The lighthouse at Gull Point was automated on a Tuesday in March, 1996, and Walter Pryce was asked to stay on for another eighteen months to make sure the machines did what they had been told. He stayed for twenty-nine years. Nobody, as far as he can tell, ever formally asked him to leave, and he never got round to it.
When I visited him in June, he was standing at the top of the tower with a cloth in one hand and a tin of brass polish in the other. The lamp no longer needs him to light it, or to wind the clockwork that once turned it, or to watch it through the night. But the brass still tarnishes in the salt air, and somebody has to deal with that.
“People think the job was about the light,” he told me. “The light was the easy part. The job was about noticing things. A ship that was too close, a storm coming in sideways, a gull with a fishing hook in its foot. You can’t automate noticing.”
Pryce grew up two villages along the coast. His father fished, and his grandfather kept a smaller light on the headland that has since fallen into the sea. He applied for the Gull Point job at twenty-three, after a friend showed him the advertisement in the back of a shipping newspaper, and he was the only applicant.
The keeper’s cottage is small and very tidy. There are logbooks on every shelf, going back to the year he arrived, each one filled with weather readings, ship sightings and, increasingly over the years, notes about birds. He has recorded more than two hundred species from the gallery of the tower.
The maritime authority that owns the lighthouse has offered, more than once, to find him somewhere more comfortable to live. He has turned them down politely each time. He pays a peppercorn rent, keeps the paint fresh and sends them his logbook entries every month, which they file somewhere and, he suspects, never read.
As I was leaving, he asked whether I would like to see the lamp lit. It was still daylight, so he put his hand over the photocell, and the great lens began to turn. “There,” he said, satisfied. “Still works.”
